findings.title: EX_INDEX / EX_SLICE never reject a nullable reference: `p[i]` on `?ref [N]T` dereferences null with no diagnostic
findings.why: `rejectNullableDeref` is the compiler's single gate for "a `?ref T` may not be used before being proved non-null"; its own message says so ("write `if p != null { ... }` first"). It is called from exactly three places -- EX_FIELD (line 1615), EX_DEREF (line 2697) and the method call at line 3381 -- and from nowhere on the EX_INDEX path (the check is missing right after `Type *ot = checkExpr(c, e->u.index.obj);`) nor on the EX_SLICE path (`Type *ot = checkExpr(c, e->u.slice.obj);`, line 1749). `checkExpr` returns a `TY_REF` unchanged (a reference is not a value-position error for `checkExpr`; only `checkValue` refuses it), `ttBase` then unwraps the `?ref [N]T` to the array, so the element/view path proceeds as if the pointer were non-null. Codegen turns that into `(*p).data[...]` / `&((*p).data[...])` with no null test, so the checker accepts a program whose C dereferences a null pointer. Line 1684 (not the `Type *it = checkValue(...)` at 1698) is where the guard belongs, because the `[]`-overload check above it also runs on the unchecked base type.
findings.trigger: `var p: ?ref [4]i32 = null` followed by `p[1]` (read or store) or `p[0..2]`. The same hole applies to a `?ref T` whose `T` is a view (`p[i]`, `p[a..b]`), and to a nullable reference that is only null on some path (`if c { p = null } ... p[0]`).
findings.repro:
cat > /tmp/ce2/nullcrash.extc <<'EOF'
fn main() -> i32 {
    var a: [4]i32 = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    var p: ?ref [4]i32 = null
    return p[1]
}
EOF
./build/extc /tmp/ce2/nullcrash.extc -o /tmp/ce2/nullcrash.c   # rc=0, NO error; generated line 131:
#   return (*p).data[extc_checkedIndex((int64_t)(1), 4, "/tmp/ce2/nullcrash.extc", 4)];
gcc -fsanitize=address,undefined -fwrapv -O1 -w -o /tmp/ce2/nullcrash /tmp/ce2/nullcrash.c
/tmp/ce2/nullcrash
#  /tmp/ce2/nullcrash.extc:4:21: runtime error: member access within null pointer of type 'struct array_4_i32'
#  AddressSanitizer:DEADLYSIGNAL ... ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000004
# Slice variant: `let s: slice<i32> = p[0..2]` also compiles (generated `&((*p).data[1])`) and traps at run
# time -- it proves the checker, not the runtime, is the missing guard.

findings.title: unifyTParams cannot unify an enum instance: a generic function with an `option<T>` / `result<T,E>` parameter can never be called
findings.why: The parameter type `option<T>` and the argument type `option<i64>` are both `TY_ENUM` (an instance built by `ttEnumGeneric`), not `TY_GENERIC`. `unifyTParams` (src/check_top.c:4637) recurses only for `want->kind == TY_REF && got->kind == TY_REF` and `want->kind == TY_GENERIC && got->kind == TY_GENERIC`; an enum instance therefore falls through to `if (ttHasParam(want)) return false;` (src/check_top.c:4644), which reports "cannot infer" even though the shapes match perfectly and the type argument is right there in `t->targs`. `result<T, E>` fails the same way. The diagnostic is also wrong in a second way: writing the arguments out does not help, because `written` only *seeds* the slots (line 3138) and the unification of the same argument still returns false -- so the compiler rejects the program no matter how the call is spelled. The mechanism is missing, not the evidence.
findings.trigger: Any generic free function whose parameter list mentions a generic **enum** instance: `fn f<T>(o: option<T>) -> T` called as `f(o)` or `f<i64>(o)` with `let o: option<i64> = option<i64>::some(i64(3))`. The pattern is the natural way to write a helper over `varArray::get` / `hashMap::get` (both return `?V`), over `?ref T` accessors, and over `result<T,E>`.

findings.title: `domain::single(...)`: a @builtin with no body skips argument checking, so extra arguments are silently discarded (side effects included)
findings.why: The branch returns the declared return type before any argument check runs -- neither the arity check of the ordinary call path (`e->u.call.args.len != f->params.len`) nor the per-argument `checkAssignable` loop. `stdlib/std/sys/domain.extc:28` declares `fn single() -> domain effects Thread=1`, so every extra argument is dropped on the floor: the arguments are never type-checked, never emitted (codegen prints the bare `extc_dom_new()`, codegen.c:2273), and therefore never evaluated. Every other builtin on this path is arity-checked -- `isViewOfDecl` at line 2998 and the `parallel::run` branch at line 3058 both test `args.len` -- so this one is an oversight, not a policy. A call whose evaluation is silently dropped is worse than a wrong diagnostic (the same reasoning the compiler applies to `parallel::run` at codegen.c:2270).
findings.trigger: `domain::single(a, b)` / `domain::single(f())` for any number of arguments. The dropped argument may be a call with a side effect, so the program does something different from what it reads as.

findings.title: EX_ASSOC's `parallel::run` branch reads the wrong union member (`e->u.call.args` on an EX_ASSOC node); it is unreachable today and would dereference NULL if it ever ran
findings.why: The node here is an EX_ASSOC (`switch (e->kind)` / `case EX_ASSOC:` at line 1935), where the argument vector is `e->u.assoc.args`; `e->u.call.callee`/`args` is the **EX_CALL** union member. The offset of `u.call.args` lands on `u.assoc.targs`, which the parser leaves empty for a non-generic callee (`parseAssoc`: `isCall = !targs.len && at(p, "(")`), so `vecAt(...,0)` would return NULL and `wa->kind` would fault. The block is currently dead for two independent reasons, both confirmed by instrumentation: `parallel::run(...)` is rewritten to an EX_CALL by the loader (`rwQualified`, src/modules.c:1053-1058) before the checker runs, and `f->isBuiltin && f->name == "parallel$run"` never survives to this switch. This is a copy of the live block in `case EX_CALL:` (line 3027), which spells `e->u.call.args` correctly. The risk is the next edit that makes the branch reachable: it is 90 lines of duplicated, untested code sitting in a path that looks live.
findings.trigger: Not reachable in the current tree (verified: `DBG_ASSOC_ENTRY` fires for `pcg32::withStream` and `box::make`, but never for `parallel::run`, and moving the name check aside does not change that). It becomes a compiler crash the moment the loader stops rewriting the call, or the branch is used for another builtin.
findings.repro: Reachability was measured, not assumed: a temporary `fprintf` at the head of `case EX_ASSOC:` (line 1935) printed only `typeName=pcg32 name=withStream` for `parallel::run(...)`, `domain::single(...)` and `box<T>::make(...)` programs, i.e. the assoc switch is never entered for these callees; the source was restored and `build/extc` rebuilt clean (the `parallel::run` conformance case in tools/attack.py lines 789-825 still passes).

findings.title: `@private` is enforced for fields, methods and operators but not for associated functions: `mod::Type::secret()` is callable from any module
findings.why: The lookup matches on `isAssoc` + name and never consults `m->isPrivate` or `m->modName`, although every other member access does: private fields are rejected in EX_FIELD (line 1640), private methods in EX_METHOD (line 3385), and private operators because `findOp` filters them (verified: a `@private fn ==` is reported as "`lib::widget` does not define `==`"). The module gate that would normally stop the call -- `rwQualified`'s `unitFunc`/visibility test -- only runs for the *function* form `mod::fn`; `mod::Type::assoc` goes through `rwQualifiedTypeName` and rewrites `typeName` to the mangled `lib$widget` without any per-member visibility check (src/modules.c:889-897). So `@private` on an associated function is documentation only, and the encapsulation the annotation promises (and that the diagnostic text states) does not hold.
findings.trigger: Module `lib` declares `struct widget { @private fn secret() -> i64 { ... } }`; another module writes `lib::widget::secret()`. Verified with the generic spelling too: `struct widget<T>` + `widget<i64>::secret()` from a file that imports the module but not the type.

coverage_notes:
Range read in full (src/check_expr.c:1421-2840), in three passes with the helpers it calls (asIntLit, repeatablePure, viewElemOf, findMethod, findOp, rejectNullableDeref, adoptContextType, ttResolve, ttSubstitute, unifyTParams, parseAssoc/rwQualified, codegen EX_INDEX/EX_SLICE/EX_CALL). Units: the tail of EX_BIN (`==`/ordering/bitwise/stream operators, 1421-1557), EX_UN, EX_FIELD (incl. field narrowing and `@private`), EX_INDEX, EX_SLICE, EX_ARRAYLIT, EX_REF, EX_TRY, EX_ASSOC (builtin `@builtin` dispatch incl. the parallel::run block), EX_CONV, EX_NEW, EX_GENCALL (`alloc`, pool primitives, generic free function, generic-type constructor), EX_COALESCE, EX_SIGN, EX_DEREF, EX_ENUMVAL, and EX_CALL up to line 2840 (the `print`/`println` deprecation warning).

Checked and found correct (not reported): fixed-array literal index bounds (asIntLit at 1732 covers `-1`; `a[-1]`, `a[4]` rejected; huge literals are refused earlier by the lexer) and the runtime guards that back it up (`extc_checkedIndex` traps, measured: `a[-1]` with a variable index prints "trap: index -1 out of range"); slice-bound checks 1793-1818 agree exactly with `extc_checkedRange` (0 <= lo <= hi <= n); `[]`-overload rewriting to EX_METHOD gets the full method machinery (arity, private check via the method path, return type) -- `v[5]` on a struct with `fn [](self: ref m, k: i64)` works, and a `@private fn []` is rejected across modules; the `isPlace` rule for slicing an array versus a view; the EX_ARRAYLIT element/length checks incl. `...` and the empty-literal diagnostic; EX_REF's `addressed`/`unNarrow` bookkeeping; EX_NEW and `alloc` level symmetry (ARENA_HOME vs block level, `minAt = -1`, registration in `curArenaSites`); `new T[n]` inside a generic (`box<T>::withCap`) works; the EX_GENCALL union-copy ordering before `e->kind = EX_ASSOC` (2461-2470) is correct; the constructor lookup at 2451 does test `m->isAssoc` (an instance method named `new` is correctly not picked as the constructor, verified); explicit type arguments do seed inference (`mkOf<i64>()`, `maxOf<i32>(4,3)` both work); EX_CONV's pointer-to-integer rule never sees a nullable ref on that line (`checkExpr` rejects it earlier with its own message); EX_SIGN / EX_DEREF / EX_ENUMVAL payload substitution and `checkEscape`; EX_CALL's lambda-receiver rewrite, `checkCallThroughFn`, and the qualified-call `isDomSingleDecl` branch.

Formatting/dead-code notes not worth a finding: the EX_ASSOC and EX_CALL blocks of the `parallel::run`/`domain::single` machinery are 90-line near-duplicates (only one of each pair is live); `case EX_CONV` reads `e->u.conv.typeName` while an unrelated branch writes `e->u.conv.type`.

Not confirmable / outside this unit: (a) whether the compiler considers private-associated-function access a deliberate relaxation (the annotation's own message says it is not, but no design doc was checked); (b) `unifyTParams` is defined in src/check_top.c:4621, outside the assigned range -- reported through its call site in this unit (src/check_expr.c:3150) with the failing line pointed at; (c) a fixed array literal can be indexed with an out-of-range constant (`[i64(1),i64(2)][5]` free of diagnostics) because `ob` is the literal's inferred `[2]i64` and no array bounds check sits on the array-literal path -- runtime still traps; not verified in a compiled form; (d) the parser does not accept a module-qualified generic association `lib::widget<i64>::secret()`, reporting "`i64` is a type, not a value" -- a diagnostic/grammar issue whose code is in src/parser.c, outside this unit.

Environment note: no compiler source change is left behind. `src/check_expr.c` was temporarily instrumented to measure EX_ASSOC reachability, then restored with `git checkout -- src/check_expr.c` and `build/extc` rebuilt clean (`git status` for src/ is empty, no DBG strings in the binary).
